blocks.text: After the Sampo was lost, old Louhi of the Northland tried to take her revenge on Kalevala. First she sent nine illnesses, but Väinämöinen drove them away. Then she sent Otso the great bear, but Väinämöinen killed it.

When both those dangers were over, Väinämöinen played on his kantele so sweetly that the Sun and the Moon came down from the sky to listen. But wicked Louhi crept up on them and caught them both, and carried them off to the Northland, and hid them in a cave deep inside a mountain. Then she crept back to Kalevala and stole all the fire from people's hearths. Now the whole world was dark, and cold, and even great Ukko, the god of the sky, did not know what to do.

Ukko searched all over the clouds for the Sun and the Moon. At last he swung his fiery sword around his head, so that lightning flashed across the sky. And from the lightning he lit a little fire. He put it in a cradle of gold and silver, and gave it to the maidens of the sky to rock and look after, so that it would grow into a new Sun. But one day the maidens weren't watching, and the fire child escaped. It burst through the clouds with a noise like thunder, and shot across the sky like a red ball of fire.
"Come on," said Väinämöinen to Ilmarinen. "Let's go and see what that fire is that has fallen from the sky."
So they set out. They came to a wide river, and made a magic boat to cross it. On the other side they met the oldest of the sky maidens.

"The fire child escaped from us," she told them, "and burst through the clouds and came down into the Northland. It did terrible harm there, until it was driven away by magic. Then it ran away, burning fields and forests as it went, until it fell into a great lake and made the water boil. The fish all met together to decide what to do, and a whiting swallowed the fire. But then the whiting had a terrible pain, until a trout swallowed it. Then the trout had the pain, until a pike swallowed the trout. And now the pike is swimming about in agony, and nobody can help it."
So Väinämöinen and Ilmarinen made a net out of seaweed, and dragged it through the lake to catch the fire fish. But the net was too weak, and the pike got away.

So they decided to grow some flax to make a stronger net. They had to go all the way to the land of the dead to find the right seed, where it was looked after by a tiny insect. They planted it on the shore, and in a single night the flax grew up and ripened. They pulled it and washed it and combed it, and the girls of Kalevala spun it and wove it into a net.

They dragged the new net through the lake. But they only caught ordinary fish. They made the net longer and wider and tried again, but still the fire fish hid in the deep. Then Väinämöinen prayed to Ahti, the god of the sea, and to his wife, to drive the fire fish into the net. And at once a little dwarf rose up out of the water and offered to help them. While they pulled the net, the dwarf beat the water with a magic pole and drove the fish towards them, and Väinämöinen sang a magic song.

This time the net was full of pike, and among them was the fire fish. Väinämöinen opened it up. Inside the pike was the trout, and inside the trout was the whiting, and inside the whiting was a ball of blue wool. Inside the blue ball was a red ball. And inside the red ball was the fire.

"How shall we carry it home?" they wondered. Ilmarinen picked it up in his hands. But it singed Väinämöinen's beard and burned Ilmarinen's hands, and then it jumped away and rolled off over the fields and forests, burning everything in its way. Väinämöinen ran after it, and at last he found it hiding in a lump of dry, rotten wood. So he put it, wood and all, in a copper box, and hurried home. And that is how fire came back to Kalevala.
Poor Ilmarinen ran down to the sea to cool his burnt hands. He called on the ice and frost and snow to cool them, and at last he prayed to Ukko, and Ukko healed them.

But even though the fire had come back, the Moon and the Sun were still missing. Frost killed the crops, and the animals began to starve, and every living thing felt sick and faint in the dark. So one of the girls of Kalevala told Ilmarinen to make a new moon out of gold and a new sun out of silver, and hang them up in the sky. Ilmarinen started work.
"That's silly," said Väinämöinen. "Silver and gold can't shine like the real sun and moon." And he was right. When Ilmarinen had made them and hung them up in the sky, they gave no light at all.

So Väinämöinen decided to find out where the real Sun and Moon had gone. He cut three chips of wood from an alder tree, and sang magic songs over them. Then he asked them where the Sun and Moon were hidden. And the alder chips told him: in a cave in the mountains of the Northland.

So Väinämöinen set off for the Northland. On the third day he came to a wide river with no boat to cross it. He lit a great fire on the bank, and the smoke rose up so high that Louhi sent a man to see what it was. Väinämöinen called out to him to bring a boat. But the man ran back to tell Louhi that Väinämöinen was coming.

So Väinämöinen turned himself into a pike, and swam across the river, and turned back into himself on the other side. Then he strode on to Louhi's house. They welcomed him as if he were an honoured guest. But as soon as he was inside, he found himself surrounded by warriors with swords and spears.
"Why have you come here?" they asked.
"I have come for the Sun and the Moon," said Väinämöinen bravely.
"We have them locked up safe in a mountain," said the chief of the warriors, "and you will never get them back. And you will never leave this hall alive!"
But Väinämöinen drew his magic sword, and fought his way out into the courtyard, and there he fought them all, and beat them all.

Then he went to find the Sun and the Moon. He came to a birch tree, and beside it a carved stone pillar. He struck the pillar three times with his sword, and it broke into pieces, and behind it was a way into the rock. But the way was shut by a great door, with only a little crack to peep through. And through the crack he could see the Sun and the Moon, locked inside. He pushed and pulled, and sang all his magic songs, but the door would not move.
So Väinämöinen hurried home to ask Ilmarinen for help, and Ilmarinen started to make a whole bunch of keys, so that one of them would be sure to open the door.

Meanwhile, old Louhi was getting worried. She turned herself into an eagle, and flew to Kalevala to see what was going on. She heard Ilmarinen hammering away, and landed on the window of his workshop.
"What are you making?" she asked.
"I'm making a steel collar for the neck of wicked old Louhi," said clever Ilmarinen, "to chain her to the rocks."

Louhi was terrified. She flew straight home to the Northland and let the Sun and the Moon out at once, and sent them back up to their places in the sky. And the sunlight and the moonlight shone on Kalevala again, and Väinämöinen and Ilmarinen and all the people prayed that they would never lose the Sun and the Moon again.

A simplified retelling of R. Eivind's “Louhi Steals the Sun and Moon” in Finnish Legends for English Children (1893). The original is listed under Other versions. Eivind spells Väinämöinen as Wainamoinen, and the sea god Ahti as Ahto.
